title: Fold Like a NASA Engineer: It's National Paper Airplane Day!
summary:
Have you ever made a paper airplane and watched it soar across the room? May 26 is National Paper Airplane Day—a whole day to celebrate these folded flyers! People have been making them for over 167 years. The first instructions for a paper dart appeared in a children's book way back in 1859. The name "paper airplane" came later, in 1907. 

Folding paper planes is sometimes called aerogami, like origami (the Japanese art of paper folding). It probably started in ancient China, where paper was invented around 105 CE. But Japan may have perfected the folding. 

If you want to make a super-cool plane, NASA can help! The first "A" in NASA stands for aeronautics—the science of flight. They have step-by-step guides to make a colorful paper airplane, plus models of NASA's X-57 Maxwell and X-59 Quiet SuperSonic Technology planes. 

Think you can break a world record? In 2022, Kim Kyu Tae threw a paper airplane 252.6 feet—that's longer than a basketball court! The longest time a paper plane stayed in the air is 31.2 seconds, set by a team in China. So grab some paper and start folding. Happy National Paper Airplane Day!
why_it_matters: Folding paper airplanes can teach you basic flight science and is a simple craft you can do with just a piece of paper at home or school.

background_read: Paper airplanes aren’t just toys—before building real airplanes, inventors like the Wright brothers used paper models to test their ideas.
NASA (the American space agency) also studies aeronautics, or the science of flight, and has made paper airplane designs for fun and learning.
Long ago, people in ancient China invented paper around 105 CE, and folding it into shapes became an art in Japan.
Article_Structure: WHO: Kids, families, NASA engineers, and record-breaker Kim Kyu Tae.
WHAT: Celebrating paper airplanes on National Paper Airplane Day, May 26.
WHERE: The tradition began in ancient China, but the day is global.
WHY: Because folding and flying paper planes is a fun way to explore aerogami and maybe break a world record.

perspectives.description: Kids and teachers love it because it’s a hands-on way to learn about aerodynamics without computers.
Some people think it’s silly to have a day for such a simple thing, but supporters say it’s a joyful break.
